newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU gives lukewarm signal for Egypt wheat tender.
newsitem.headline: EU gives lukewarm signal for Egypt wheat tender.

text.p: French wheat prices were flat to slightly firmer on Friday as the market gave a mixed reaction to the previous day's European Union export award, EU traders said.
The EU granted licences for 249,800 tonnes of wheat at a maximum refund of 14.98 Ecus per tonne.

With the market focusing on a key weekend tender from Egypt for March and April wheat, traders said a recovery in EU exports from the previous week was a positive sign but refunds were still inadequate to give them much of a chance with Egypt.
Traders said they would need something like 17 or 18 Ecus per tonne to knock out competition for what could be one of the last substantial single purchases of old crop wheat.
Rouen-delivered wheat for February gained five francs a tonne to 860 francs at private stores but remained stuck at 855 francs at public silos, operators said. Prices exclude carry.
On the previous Thursday, Brussels had surprised the market by releasing around 72,000 tonnes of wheat at a maximum rebate of 14.50 Ecus per tonne.

This week's quantity did not fully compensate for the temporary slowdown on January 23 -- the EU says its average export pace has been 300,000 or 400,000 tonnes a week -- but traders called the higher refund a step in the right direction.
"We were afraid Brussels had got stuck at 14.50 Ecus. This slight rise of yesterday is fairly encouraging, especially when you are covering upcoming business," one trader said.
Egypt is in the market for Argentine, U.S. or French wheat and could end up buying 800,000 tonnes overall, shippers say. French exporters hope to get 200-300,000 tonnes.

But one trader suggested Thursday's EU award was in fact a disappointment for anyone seeking to supply Egypt. French wheat prices of $150 per tonne implied by Thursday's award had little chance, he said. "We have had no signal telling us to sell to Egypt."
Traders said French EU-subsidised wheat would have to drop to somewhere between $145 and $146 a tonne, closer to its paper value, to be considered seriously for Egypt.
That left some uncertainty over whether Europe-based firms would leave themselves vulnerable to Brussels by making aggressive offers to Egypt.

That country's tender is the plum prospect on an otherwise dreary export scene and traders will have to second-guess whether the Commission is ready to push out wheat to cover a sale or sit back and keep up the pressure on domestic prices.
